documents: Published paper: Raad et al. (2023) Basin Research 35:1-27, PDF (27 pages)

entry.evidence: The mechanisms and time spans for the deposition of the MSC evaporites are still not clear and highly debated

steps.action: The authors take over their own earlier seismic-stratigraphic interpretation of the CMD MSC units (BU1, BU2, salt, BU3) as an undeformed analogue of the Caltanissetta Basin.
steps.quote: showed that the MSC evaporitic sequence in the CMD could be an undeformed analogue of the intermediate-depth Caltanissetta Basin in Sicily

steps.action: The authors set two objectives: the hydrological conditions (salinity, fluxes) under which CMD gypsum and halite formed, and the amplitude of drawdown needed to explain them.
steps.quote: establish the hydrological conditions (salinity and fluxes) and mechanisms under which the evaporites (gypsum and halite) in the CMD formed

steps.action: The authors use their own earlier flexural-isostatic backstripping of the pre-MSC paleo-bathymetry to give the CMD hypsometry and sill depths (850 and 750 m).
steps.quote: restoration of the Messinian paleo-topography of a large area in the Western Mediterranean, including the BP

steps.action: The authors compute unit volumes from seismic thickness maps, using interval velocities for time-to-depth conversion and assumed evaporite/clastic ratios (80% gypsum for BU1/2, 50% for BU3, 100% halite).
steps.quote: We use widespread high- and low-resolution seismic reflection profiles to calculate the volumes of the MSC units in the CMD

steps.action: The authors derive box-model relations from conservation of water and salt (Vmin, freshwater budget, salinity evolution, Knudsen relation, precipitation rates and durations).
steps.quote: One of these principles is the conservation of water volume for a system that is in balance.

steps.action: The authors pose three rival connection configurations between the CMD and the Mediterranean: no connection, blocked outflow (inflow only), and two-way exchange.
steps.quote: Different ways to approach the connection between the CMD and the open Mediterranean.

steps.action: The authors compare the saturated-water volumes needed for the observed gypsum and halite with the reconstructed CMD water volume below sill depth (Figure 5, Table 4).
steps.quote: we calculate the volumes of water required to precipitate the observed volume of evaporites

steps.action: The authors exclude a disconnected basin as the source of the gypsum, since it yields only 0.9% of the observed volume, while keeping it viable for halite (141%).
steps.quote: the gypsum deposit is too massive to originate from a disconnected basin, even if it was saturated in gypsum

steps.action: The authors model desiccation of an isolated CMD for river inflow R = 0, 1 and 10 m3/s and find a new equilibrium within about 1 kyr (Figure 6).
steps.quote: The fastest change occurs in an extreme scenario without any river input at all

steps.action: The authors check that even high river inflow reduces the halite precipitated on desiccation by a negligible amount relative to the observed volume.
steps.quote: this effect is small enough to be ignored

steps.action: The authors compute the fastest salinity rise for a full basin with inflow only, for the CMD and the Valencia Basin, under two inflow salinities and two E-P values (Figure 7, Table 5).
steps.quote: we consider the fastest change in concentration possible for a basin with constant volume

steps.action: The authors exclude the blocked-outflow scenario for gypsum, because halite saturation would be reached (21 kyr) long before the gypsum volume could precipitate (182 kyr).
steps.quote: halite cannot have formed by the same mechanism (i.e., blocked outflow)

steps.action: After the inflow-only failure, the authors model two-way exchange and compute the maximal outflux compatible with gypsum saturation as a function of inflow salinity and water level (Figure 8).
steps.quote: To explore this new scenario, we now quantify the size of the volume flux of water out of the basin

steps.action: The authors compare the required fluxes with present-day measured exchange (ca. 0.1 Sv) and conclude that the inflowing Mediterranean water must already be near gypsum saturation.
steps.quote: the only way for the CMD to reach gypsum saturation is when the salinity of the surface to intermediate layer

steps.action: The authors estimate gypsum precipitation duration per precessional cycle from outflux and inflow salinity, filtered by realistic precipitation rates of 1 to 100 m/kyr (Figure 9).
steps.quote: the duration of precipitation itself ranges between 0.8 and 5 kyr per cycle

steps.action: The authors test the effect of a 30% underestimation of the gypsum volume on the precipitation-duration result.
steps.quote: Even an underestimation of 30% of the gypsum volume would only have a noticeable influence on the duration of precipitation

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that the upper layer of the open Western Mediterranean reached gypsum saturation during the dry phases of stage 1 cycles.
steps.quote: the saturation concentration of gypsum must have been reached in the upper layers of the open Western Mediterranean

steps.action: The authors set the claim against cited foraminiferal evidence and earlier box-model results showing rapid salinity rise to gypsum saturation.
steps.quote: Topper and Meijer (2015) showed that the salinity of the open Mediterranean waters could rise to gypsum saturation

steps.action: The authors reject the rival view that gypsum saturation and PLG deposition required shallow silled marginal basins, using the deep-silled CMD as a counterexample.
steps.quote: Our result, thus, contradicts what has been proposed by Lugli et al. (2010)

steps.action: The authors pose three rival halite scenarios: drawdown and disconnection at sill depth, a stratified full basin with deep brine, and a chance match of volumes.
steps.quote: Three possible scenarios can reproduce our observations

steps.action: The authors evaluate scenario 1 against model results: with inflow near gypsum saturation and blocked outflow, halite saturation is reached in about 1 kyr, followed by rapid quasi-desiccation.
steps.quote: the time to reach halite saturation can be as short as 1 kyr

steps.action: The authors reject the stratified-basin scenario because of basin size and connection, and because it would overproduce halite within about 2 kyr.
steps.quote: such a scenario is unlikely to take place in the CMD

steps.action: The authors reject the connected, halite-saturated basin scenario, since it would need unrealistically slow horizontal velocities or would overproduce halite.
steps.quote: hinting again that the CMD has to disconnect from the Mediterranean

steps.action: The authors check the quasi-desiccation result against independent observations: the erosion surface on top of the CMD halite and the desiccation surface in the Caltanissetta salt.
steps.quote: Our results supporting a quasi-desiccation of the CMD seem consistent with previously reported [...] .

steps.action: The authors apply the inflow-only calculation to the whole Mediterranean during stage 2 and find it would yield 1.5 times the observed deep-basin evaporite volume.
steps.quote: Results of our calculations show that we would precipitate x1.5 times the observed deep basin evaporite volume

steps.action: The authors use the reconstructed Western Mediterranean hypsometry to estimate the starting salinity and drawdown needed to form the deep-basin halite volume (Figure 11).
steps.quote: This volume is only reached for a water column that starts precipitating after a drawdown of ca. 700 m or sooner

steps.action: The authors conclude that CMD halite formed after a drawdown of at least about 850 m that disconnected the CMD, following gypsum deposition under two-way exchange.
steps.quote: the drawdown reached the depth of the basin sill lying at ca. 850 mbsl, leading to the complete disconnection of the CMD

steps.action: The authors refine the 3-stage consensus model by flagging PLG restricted to shallow silled basins and synchronous RLG and halite onset as needing reconsideration.
steps.quote: our results also highlight that some aspects of such model (e.g., limiting the PLG deposition to shallow >200m silled basins

Limited sensitivity tests (river inflow, E-P, drawdown, gypsum volume, sill depth)
Gypsum: two-way exchange with near-saturated Mediterranean; halite: disconnection after drawdown of at least 850 m
No review file supplied; referees only acknowledged

end.claim: The CMD gypsum requires two-way exchange with a Mediterranean upper layer near gypsum saturation, while the CMD halite requires disconnection of the basin by a drawdown of at least ca. 850 m (sill depth).

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the observed evaporite volumes with the saturated water volume the reconstructed CMD holds below sill depth separates gypsum (0.9%, needs exchange) from halite (141%, consistent with disconnection); every later scenario test builds on that split.

gates.evidence: The seismic data and paleo-bathymetry were acquired and interpreted in earlier studies, not directed by the connection hypotheses. Each scenario could fail a volumetric or timing test, and several did (disconnected basin for gypsum, inflow-only, halite scenarios 2 and 3). The surviving scenario was judged by consistency, not by a decisive independent test. No pre-registration or fixed thresholds are reported; precipitation-rate filters were taken from the literature.

imports.item: conservation of mass of water and salt (box-model formulation)
salinity tolerance of planktic foraminifera from laboratory cultures (Bijma et al., 1990)

novelty_claims.quote: In this study, we scale down as we apply models based on conservation of mass of water and salt
To our knowledge, until present, no studies showed or quantified such a decrease in the Mediterranean currents and its consequences during the MSC.
our calculation could be considered an improvement to Krijgsman and Meijer (2008)

limits:
Only the published paper was supplied; no review file, so no review sequence. The data are available only on request.

The seismic interpretation and the paleo-bathymetry are inherited from the authors' earlier work and are not re-tested here.

Uncertainties are handled only through scattered sensitivity statements: river inflow, E-P, drawdown, a 30% gypsum-volume error, and the 800 vs 850 m sill. The halite volume error (±5%) is asserted, not computed. Parameters such as seawater composition, evaporation rates (present-day values) and the strait parameter carry no propagated uncertainty.

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Upper Western Mediterranean at gypsum saturation in stage 1: best_explanation.
- Gypsum precipitation lasting 5-20% of a precessional cycle: estimate_with_resolution, given as a range without formal uncertainty.
- PLG not limited to shallow silled basins (against Lugli et al. 2010): best_explanation.
- Western Mediterranean deep-basin halite needing an average starting salinity of at least 232 kg/m3 or a drawdown of about 1600 m at saturation: estimate_with_resolution, with a simplistic uniform water column.
- Whole-Mediterranean disconnection during stage 2: best_explanation, with the simplifications the authors acknowledge.

Inference: the order of scenarios (inflow-only, then two-way exchange) is presented as a logical progression; the paper does not say whether it reflects the actual research sequence.

disagreements.target: Lugli et al. (2010): gypsum saturation only in silled marginal basins
disagreements.support: Box-model fluxes for the deep-silled, wide-channel CMD require the open Mediterranean upper layer at gypsum saturation, so no shallow sill is needed; the authors add that PLG is recovered offshore on open shelves.
disagreements.quote: Our result, thus, contradicts what has been proposed by Lugli et al. (2010)

disagreements.target: 3-stage MSC consensus model (CIESM, 2008; Roveri, Flecker, et al., 2014)
disagreements.support: The CMD gypsum volume and fluxes imply PLG deposition beyond shallow silled basins and RLG formation not tied to stage 2; the authors say much of the model is otherwise coherent with their results.
disagreements.quote: some aspects of such model (e.g., limiting the PLG deposition to shallow >200m [...] basins; and the synchronous onset of the RLG and halite)

disagreements.target: RLG formed during stage 2 (Manzi, Roveri, et al., 2021; Roveri et al., 2006)
disagreements.support: Argued from gravitational instability and cited Cyprus observations (Artiaga et al., 2021) that resedimentation could occur at any time after deposition.
disagreements.quote: [...] happened in any moment after the gypsum's deposition and not necessarily during stage 2 of the MSC

disagreements.target: Interpretations of distal stage 1 equivalents as organic shales, not gypsum (Manzi et al., 2018; Manzi, Roveri, et al., 2021; Dela Pierre et al., 2011)
disagreements.support: The authors cite later reinterpretations (Natalicchio et al., 2021; Meilijson et al., 2018) and unpublished XRD data on sulphate inclusions, alongside their model of widespread gypsum deposition.
disagreements.quote: contradicts the presence of gypsum in the distal domain of such basins

disagreements.target: Halite deposition starting in stage 1 (Meilijson et al., 2018, 2022)
disagreements.support: Their CMD and Western Mediterranean volume calculations indicate halite started only after drawdown began, while admitting the eastern basin may differ.
disagreements.quote: strongly indicate that halite did not start depositing before the beginning of the drawdown.

disagreements.target: Krijgsman and Meijer (2008) whole-Mediterranean halite volume calculation
disagreements.support: The same approach with the Haq et al. (2020) volume yields 1.5 times or more the observed volume, which they call an improvement rather than a contradiction.
disagreements.quote: This is not a contradiction to the results of Krijgsman and Meijer (2008)

disagreements.target: Raad et al. (2021): subaerial exposure and/or dissolution at the top-halite erosion surface
disagreements.support: The desiccation model shows river input prevents complete desiccation, so shallow subaqueous erosion is preferred.
disagreements.quote: the subaqueous but shallow origin should be preferred
